passage:
"Who was that?" Lavanya asked as Sarvesh put his phone face down.
"My cousin. About Sunday lunch."
"You turned it over."
"Because last time you read my messages, Lavanya. I just want one thing that's mine."
"If there's nothing to hide, why do you need a thing that's yours?"
Sarvesh rubbed his eyes. "I haven't done anything. For months I've explained every late reply, every photo. I'm tired of being on trial."
"And I'm tired of you hiding."
"I'm not hiding! I'm protecting myself."
Lavanya's mother called from the kitchen, "Dinner's getting cold, you two."
Neither moved. Sarvesh took his phone to the balcony. Lavanya watched the closed glass door and felt her fears grow louder with every minute he stayed out there.

qa.q: Who did Sarvesh say had messaged him?
qa.a: He said it was his cousin, about Sunday lunch.

qa.q: How does Sarvesh feel about being questioned again?
qa.a: He feels distrusted without reason and exhausted, saying he is tired of being on trial.

qa.q: What turning point could break this loop?
qa.a: One of them could pause and name the pattern out loud, for example that his privacy feels like hiding to her and her questions feel like accusation to him, instead of defending their own side.

qa.q: How does Lavanya read Sarvesh going to the balcony?
qa.a: She takes it as more proof he is hiding something, which makes her fears grow while he only wanted space.

grounding: It shows a partner who feels distrusted and keeps more privacy, which the other reads as hiding, so each one's protection confirms the other's fear.

passage:
I'm Imran, and this is about last winter with Rehana.
At first I didn't mind her questions. Where were you, who was that. I answered, even showed my phone once. But it never ended. One night she asked why I'd smiled at a text, and something in me went cold. I thought: I have done nothing, and I'm still guilty.
So I started keeping things to myself. I changed my phone lock. I went for long walks alone. It felt like breathing room. To Rehana it looked exactly like a man with a secret.
The more she pushed, the more I closed; the more I closed, the more she pushed. Looking back, we were both scared, and we were both making it worse.

qa.q: What did Imran change on his phone?
qa.a: He changed his phone lock.

qa.q: What did Imran feel the night Rehana asked why he smiled at a text?
qa.a: He felt something go cold, a mix of hurt and resentment at being treated as guilty when he had done nothing.

qa.q: What could Imran have tried instead of quietly closing off?
qa.a: He could have told Rehana calmly that her checking made him feel distrusted and that his walks were for breathing room, so his privacy did not look like a secret.

qa.q: How did Rehana likely see Imran's long walks alone?
qa.a: She probably saw them as proof that he was hiding something, which pushed her to question him even more.

grounding: It illustrates the partner's side of the spiral, where feeling wrongly distrusted leads him to guard his privacy and that guarding feeds her suspicion.

passage:
The college library in Shillong closed at eight, and Tejas had started staying till the very end.

It wasn't the work. It was that at home, in the evenings, Yangchen asked questions. Who were you with? Why did you smile at your phone? Can I see?

He had never done anything. That was what burned. For three months he had shown her every chat, answered every question, and still she looked at him like a suspect.

So he started keeping things. Not secrets, exactly. Just space. He turned his phone face down. He stopped mentioning the girls in his study group, even though they talked only about thermodynamics.

On Thursday Yangchen said, "You've changed. You're hiding things now."

"I'm not hiding. I'm tired of being searched."

She stared at him, and he could see it in her face: his tiredness had just become her proof.

qa.q: What time did the college library close?
qa.a: At eight.

qa.q: Why does Tejas stay at the library until closing?
qa.a: He feels resentful and worn out from being distrusted for nothing, and wants some private space away from Yangchen's questions.

qa.q: What could break this cycle at this stage?
qa.a: Both could name what is happening: Tejas says he feels searched and resentful, and Yangchen talks about her fear, perhaps with a counsellor's help, instead of each protecting themselves.

qa.q: How does Yangchen read Tejas's new need for space?
qa.a: She reads it as proof that he is hiding something, which deepens her fear and suspicion.

grounding: Tejas feels distrusted for nothing and starts keeping more private space, which Yangchen reads as proof of hiding, so the spiral feeds itself.

passage:
Lalremsiami,

I'm writing because when we talk, it becomes a fight within two minutes.

For six months I've answered every question. Where I was, who texted, why I took long to reply. I've handed you my phone more times than I can count. You've never found anything, because there's nothing to find.

And I'm tired. I'm angry, honestly. I feel like a suspect in my own relationship.

So yes, lately I've been keeping things to myself. I don't tell you about my evenings with the band. I put my phone on silent. Not because I'm hiding, but because I need somewhere that isn't searched.

And I know you see that as proof. I know every time I pull back, you get more scared, and then you ask more, and then I pull back more.

We're stuck. I don't know how to get out alone. Can we try talking to someone? Together?

Dhruv

qa.q: How long has Dhruv been answering every question?
qa.a: For six months.

qa.q: What is Dhruv feeling while writing this letter?
qa.a: Dhruv feels tired, angry and resentful at being treated like a suspect, while also stuck and worried about where they are heading.

qa.q: What does Dhruv suggest as a way out, and why could it help?
qa.a: Talking to someone together, like a counsellor, because the loop of fear and withdrawal is hard to break alone.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami likely see Dhruv's silence about the band evenings?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably reads it as proof that Dhruv is hiding something, which makes the fear grow.

grounding: Dhruv's letter shows Dhruv resentful at being distrusted and keeping more private space, which Lalremsiami reads as proof of hiding, so the spiral feeds itself.

passage:
You want to know how it got so bad with Saba? I'm Rafiq, and I'll tell you what I told Kishore last month.

At first I answered everything. Every "who's that?" and "why are you late?" I showed her my phone whenever she asked. I thought, if I'm open, she'll relax.

She didn't. So I got angry. Not shouting, just that slow, sour kind of anger. I thought, I've done nothing, and I'm treated like a criminal.

So I started keeping bits of my life to myself. Didn't mention when I played football with the boys. Changed my lock screen. Normal privacy, I told myself.

Of course, Saba noticed. "Why'd you change your password?" "Why didn't you tell me about football?" And every question made me pull back more.

Kishore said, "You two are protecting yourselves from each other." He was right. We'd built a trap and we were both inside it.

qa.q: What did Rafiq change that Saba noticed?
qa.a: The lock screen and the password.

qa.q: What kind of anger does Rafiq describe, and why did it build?
qa.a: A slow, sour resentment, because Rafiq felt treated like a criminal despite having done nothing.

qa.q: What could Rafiq and Saba do to get out of the trap Kishore describes?
qa.a: Talk honestly about how the questions and the pulling back feed each other, and perhaps get a counsellor's help to break the cycle.

qa.q: How does Kishore see the relationship from outside?
qa.a: Kishore sees both protecting themselves from each other, each person's defence confirming the other's fear.

grounding: Rafiq, distrusted for nothing, grows resentful and keeps more private space, which Saba reads as hiding, showing the spiral feeding itself.

passage:
Monday. Binita asked Raghav, for the third time that week, who he had been texting at lunch. "My project partner," he said, and showed her. She nodded, but didn't smile. He walked to class feeling like a suspect.
Thursday. Raghav turned his phone face down on the café table before she arrived. He hadn't done anything. He just wanted one small corner of his life that wasn't checked. When Binita noticed, her eyes narrowed. "Why's it upside down?"
"Because I'm tired of explaining," he snapped, and regretted the tone at once.
The next Sunday. He had put a lock on the phone and stopped mentioning his evening football. Binita said quietly, "You're hiding things now. I knew it."
Raghav stared at her. "I'm hiding because you keep searching."
Both of them felt completely right, and neither moved.

qa.q: What did Raghav do with his phone on Thursday before Binita arrived?
qa.a: He turned his phone face down on the café table.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when he snapped, 'Because I'm tired of explaining'?
qa.a: He felt resentful and worn out from being treated like a suspect, and then regretted his tone.

qa.q: What could interrupt this spiral at this stage?
qa.a: One of them could name the loop out loud, that his privacy is self-protection and her questions come from fear, and ask for a calm talk, perhaps with a counsellor.

qa.q: How does Binita read Raghav's new privacy?
qa.a: To Binita the phone lock and the missing football updates look like proof that he is hiding something, which feeds her fear.

grounding: Shows a young man who feels distrusted guarding more privacy, which Binita reads as hiding, so each person's protection confirms the other's story.
